newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - British authorities at odds over monetary policy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - British authorities at odds over monetary policy.

text.p: Britain's finance minister Kenneth Clarke and the Bank of England clashed publicly over monetary policy on Wednesday, with the central bank insisting interest rates needed to rise while Clarke again rejected its advice.
An unexpectedly large drop in January unemployment confirmed that the economy was powering ahead, while average earnings growth in December accelerated.

The Bank of England said in its quarterly Inflation Report that a moderate increase in interest rates was needed to ensure the government's 2.5 percent inflation target could be met in two years' time.
"The Bank's central projection for inflation two years ahead is close to three percent and rising," it said.

Underlying annual inflation, which was 3.1 percent in December, would fall this year as the strong pound made imported goods cheaper. Sterling has surged 16 percent in value against other major currencies since last summer.

"But monetary policy must look beyond these short-term effects and ensure that underlying inflation is consistent with the target," the report said. "The Bank continues to see the need for a moderate tightening of policy."
Clarke, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, has been resisting pressure from the Bank to raise rates from the present 6.0 percent since December.
He has a strong political incentive not to increase the cost of borrowing before the looming election as this would mean dearer home loans for millions of Britons.

In a series of interviews on Wednesday, the Chancellor said he disagreed with the Bank's view that action was needed now to prevent the economy overheating and he believed current economic signals were conflicting.
"I think we are recovering extremely strongly, but things have been going steadily since Christmas. They show no signs of speeding up," he said in a radio interview.
"I think it is not yet at the stage where I have to put the brakes on. I would put up interest rates now if I thought it was the right thing to do."
Clarke also said the Bank had toned down its advice since December, when George said he might have to recommend raising rates to 6.50 percent in January or February.
"The Governor has actually slightly modified and toned down his advice since the December meeting," he told ITN television.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said unemployment fell 67,800 in January to 1.815 million on a seasonally adjusted basis. This represented a jobless rate of 6.5 percent, a six-year low.
But it also said that underlying average earnings grew 4.25 percent in December and the November figure was revised up to 4.25 percent from an original estimate of 4.0 percent.
The government played down the rise in pay levels, saying it was partly due to performance-related bonuses and overtime.
But the Bank of England made clear it was concerned.
"Earnings growth rose by one percentage point over the past 12 months," chief economist Mervyn King told a news conference.
"If that were repeated over the next 12 months, which is quite likely, you get to levels that are inconsistent with meeting the inflation target."
